analysis.one_liner: Lets livestock and poultry farmers choose whether to arbitrate disputes only after a dispute arises.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee; it died at the end of 2002 without a vote, despite a bipartisan group of five senators sponsoring it.
analysis.plain_summary: Contract chicken and hog farmers typically sign contracts that force them to settle disputes with meat companies in arbitration, often with a company-chosen arbitrator and no explanation of the decision. This bill would change that: arbitration could only be used if both the farmer and the company agree after the dispute actually arises, and arbitrators would have to give a written explanation of their decision. The bill was introduced in September 2002 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it stayed until Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.who_benefits: Livestock and poultry growers — the farmers who raise chickens, hogs, and cattle under contracts with large meat companies. They would keep the right to take a dispute to court instead of being locked into arbitration by fine print they signed before any problem existed, and they would get a written explanation if arbitration is used.

how_it_helps.text: Arbitration under a livestock or poultry contract could be used only if, after a controversy arises, both parties consent in writing — meaning a farmer is not forced into arbitration by a clause signed long before the dispute.
If arbitration is used, the arbitrator must give the parties a written explanation of the factual and legal basis for the award, instead of an unexplained decision.
The rules apply to contracts entered into, renewed, or extended after enactment, so growers could not be bound by old pre-dispute arbitration clauses on renewals.

analysis.who_pays: Large meat processors, poultry integrators, and livestock packers, whose contracts currently lock growers into arbitration. Their legal teams would face more court cases from growers, and the arbitration firms that handle these disputes would handle fewer of them.

drawbacks.text: Meat companies argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper for both sides than litigation, and that mandatory court access could mean smaller farmers with weak claims suing over every disagreement — costs that could be passed back into contract terms.

The bill is narrow: it covers only livestock and poultry contracts, and only changes who consents to arbitration and what the arbitrator must write. It does not address the underlying imbalance in grower contracts, such as exclusive dealing or termination rights.
Because it applies only to new or renewed contracts, growers locked into existing long-term contracts would get no help until those contracts end.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: a specific group of farmers — poultry and livestock growers — would regain the choice of forum when disputes with large integrators arise, and gain a written reason for any arbitration award. The cost falls on large meat companies and arbitration providers, who lose a procedural home-field advantage. The bill is narrow and does not touch the broader economics of grower contracts, but its main flaw is that it never became law.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill once and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until this Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Feingold introduced the bill with Sens. Grassley, Harkin, Leahy, and Enzi on September 17, 2002, drawing sponsors from both parties.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meat and poultry processors, which kept the ability to require arbitration in grower contracts, and the arbitration firms that handle those disputes. Contract farmers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big meat processors and arbitration firms

for.name: Sen. Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Chuck Grassley and Mike Enzi
for.role: U.S. Senators from Iowa and Wyoming
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Sens. Tom Harkin and Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senators from Iowa and Vermont
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors; Leahy chaired the Judiciary Committee the bill was sent to.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, reported the bill, or moved it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor group was bipartisan — 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans among the original sponsors, and the 6 cosponsors included 4 Democrats and 2 Republicans — and no opposition vote ever occurred because the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Large meat processors and poultry integrators (chicken, hog, and cattle contracting companies)
industries.note: These companies write grower contracts with pre-dispute arbitration clauses that steer disputes away from courts. The bill would let farmers insist on a judge instead, taking away a structural advantage in disputes.
Grower disputes would only reach arbitration if both sides agree after the dispute, and any award would need a written explanation — shrinking this segment of the arbitration business.
